my_sentence: More and more companies start believe their data will help them.
correction: More and more companies start to believe their data will help them.
explanation: "Start" is followed by the infinitive "to believe" (or the gerund "believing"), not the bare verb "believe." The teacher inserted "to."
correct_examples: Companies start to believe in data.
He started to learn English last year.
context: Explaining why data scientists are in demand.

my_sentence: Being a servant is one of the worst job.
correction: Being a servant is one of the worst jobs.
explanation: After "one of the," the noun must be plural because you are picking one item out of a group: "one of the worst jobs." The teacher repeated "jobs."
correct_examples: It is one of the worst jobs.
She is one of the best students.
context: Arguing that being a servant is one of the worst jobs.

my_sentence: They have to reduce their prices to competitor with others.
correction: They have to reduce their prices to compete with others.
explanation: "Competitor" is a noun (the person/company); the verb is "compete." After "to" you need the verb "compete." The teacher said "to compete, not competitor, that's a noun."
correct_examples: They lower prices to compete with rivals.
Small firms compete with big companies.
context: Explaining why online English tutoring prices dropped.

my_sentence: I need to buy some necessary things for my family.
correction: I need to buy some things that are necessary for my family.
explanation: (assistant note) Jack's version is understandable, but the teacher modeled the smoother relative-clause phrasing "some things that are necessary for my family," which sounds more natural in speech and was drilled twice.
correct_examples: I buy things that are necessary for my family.
We only spend on things that are necessary.
